Front. Sustain. Cities, 04 November 2026

Sec. Smart Technologies and Cities

Volume 8 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/frsc.2026.1960337

An IoT based three-tier fog computing architecture for policy-aware Smart Waste Management using fog and edge

  • AK

    Adesh Kanna Prakash

  • MS

    M. Sambath *

  • AS

    Ananyaa Subramanian

  • DS

    Dhanisha Sethupathy

  • School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Chennai, India

Article metrics

View details

Abstract

Introduction:

In fast-urbanizing areas, municipal solid waste collection still runs on a fixed schedule that ignores real-time bin state, wasting fleet capacity and leaving overflow-prone bins unserviced. The main problems are as much about governance as engineering: service delivery is unlinked from need, with no accountability signal; statutory segregation duties are unenforceable for want of an evidentiary base; enforcement instruments are ungraduated; and the distributional burden is invisible. Smart-bin systems presently address sensing or routing in isolation, funneling telemetry through one cloud tier whose wide-area latency is incompatible with time-critical hazard alerts.

Methods:

We present SWMS, a three-tier edge/fog/cloud system in which smart bins sense fill level, methane, temperature, and weight, district fog nodes evaluate thresholds and compute routes locally, and a cloud tier runs graduated compliance enforcement and an Eco-Score layer. All results are computational, not measurements of a deployment. No physical prototype was deployed, and all bin data are synthetic; the compliance and gamification layers were implemented but not validated by any user study, though the sensor error model was calibrated to real gas-sensor data.

Results:

A seeded Monte Carlo model places the fog-mediated alert path at 30.9 ms against 233.1 ms for a cloud counterfactual, confirmed by two discrete-event simulations. A comparison with a proven optimal solution shows that greedy+2-opt closes to within 5.1%, matching the best tuned metaheuristic at three orders of magnitude lower compute. A service-parity comparison cuts daily collection distance by 37.9%, reproduced at 38.7% on an actual OpenStreetMap street network. Scalability to 20,000 bins follows O(n1.72), and fault injection raises overflow-alert F1 from 0.70 to 0.80 at 50% sensor faults.

Discussion:

We situate the design in the public-governance and regulatory-governance literatures and identify the obstacles a deployment faces: statutory authority, due process, administrative discretion, attribution in communal bins, distributive incidence, legitimacy, data protection, and municipal capacity. Because a non-zero sensor error rate entails a non-zero wrongful-penalty rate, we conclude that the compliance layer should first be deployed as a non-penal, evidentiary, and advisory instrument rather than a penal one.

1 Introduction

Growing urban populations and tightening sustainability constraints put increasing pressure on municipal solid waste (MSW) management. India's Central Pollution Control Board reports that urban areas generate roughly 150,000 tonnes of solid waste a day, of which under 30% is scientifically treated [Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), 2022]. Collection wastes journeys: trucks run fixed routes on fixed schedules, ignoring bin state and servicing empty bins while overflowing ones wait. The overflow causes soil pollution, vector-borne disease risk and unaccounted greenhouse-gas emissions—especially methane, whose 100-year warming potential is some 25–28 × that of CO2.

IoT sensing is a tangible response, and a growing literature instruments bins with fill-level and, more recently, gas sensors (Section 2). Two structural gaps remain. First, most deployments route all telemetry to a single cloud tier, adding wide-area latency to what should be a sub-second alert path for fire risk and toxic methane build-up. Second, sensing and routing are treated as the whole problem: telemetry drives a route, and that is it. Municipal operations also need policy—graduated enforcement for chronic non-compliance, and incentives that make compliance the easier choice. Routing optimizers that ignore compliance underuse their telemetry, and fines imposed without predictive dispatch generate friction for no benefit.

1.1 The governance problems this system addresses

Presenting this system merely as a sensing-and-routing optimization does not do justice to what municipal authorities are trying to fix. Municipal solid waste is a classic case of a public service whose failures are governance failures before they are engineering failures (Kaza et al., 2018; Guerrero et al., 2013). The technology has existed for a century, yet coverage, source segregation, and disposal standards remain poor across much of South Asia (Doron and Jeffrey, 2018; Mani and Singh, 2016): much of the waste generated stays uncollected or poorly processed. The engineering fixes exist; what shortens the shelf life of any design is institutional, regulatory, and implementation failure. We therefore state at the outset the five concrete governance problems the architecture is designed to act on, and return in Section 7 to the regulatory and policy obstacles each of them raises.

  • Allocative failure with no service-accountability signal: fleet capacity is allocated by timetable rather than by state, so trucks service empty bins while full ones wait. The core issue is informational: neither authority nor citizen holds a durable, timestamped record of which bins overflowed and for how long, so under-service is unattributable and cannot be made the object of an enforceable performance standard. Performance-based regulation relies on exactly the measurement base that is missing (Sparrow, 2000; Dunleavy et al., 2006).

  • A statutory duty without an evidentiary base: India's Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India, 2016) impose duties directly on every waste generator: Rule 4(1)(a) requires segregation into three streams and handover to authorized collectors, Rule 4(2) prohibits throwing, burning or burying waste on streets and public spaces, and Rule 4(3) obliges payment of the user fee set in local bye-laws. Rule 15(zf) in turn requires local authorities to frame bye-laws containing the criteria for levying spot fines on persons who litter or fail to comply. Urban local bodies nonetheless hold no systematic generator-level record of conduct, making enforcement episodic, discretionary, and hard to defend when contested. This is the classic regulatory-capacity problem: inspection resources are scarce, and targeting them rationally requires data the regulator does not have (Sparrow, 2000; Black and Baldwin, 2010; Hood et al., 2001).

  • Instrument-choice failure: sanction without graduation, information without escalation: where enforcement does occur, the penalty is typically flat, with no escalation path—the pattern the regulatory literature associates with resistance and legitimacy loss rather than compliance (Bardach and Kagan, 1982). Pure information campaigns, conversely, exhaust their effect quickly. Responsive regulation prescribes an enforcement pyramid: persuasion first, escalating sanctions only against persistent non-compliance (Ayres and Braithwaite, 1992); smart regulation prescribes complementary instruments mixes rather than single instruments (Gunningham et al., 1998; Hood and Margetts, 2007; Howlett, 2019). The three-warning monthly buffer followed by a graduated fine, with a positive Eco-Score incentive running in parallel (Section 3), implements that pyramid—a framing that the earlier version of this article left implicit.

  • A time-critical hazard that the administrative cycle cannot serve: a municipality can be held liable for duty-of-care hazards such as methane build-up and bin fires, but an alert path completing a wide-area round trip cannot underwrite a response-time commitment under load. Response-time standards are precisely the enforceable service obligation a regulator can write into a contract or bye-law (Baldwin et al., 2012); an architecture that demonstrably meets one is a prerequisite for writing it.

  • Distributive invisibility: without per-bin longitudinal data we cannot identify which neighborhoods absorb chronic under-service, so inequity in a basic public service persists unmeasured and uncontested. Longitudinal telemetry is thus an equity-audit instrument before it is an efficiency instrument—an application of urban data the smart-city governance literature treats as among the more justifiable (Kitchin, 2016; Meijer and Bolívar, 2016).

Put this way, the contribution is a policy instrument, not just an optimization. The reframing cuts both ways: instruments assigning burdens to identifiable people attract legal, procedural, and distributive constraints that an optimizer does not, and Section 7 treats those as design requirements rather than deployment details.

1.2 Positioning and contributions

We do not claim novelty in any single sensing, routing, or fog-placement technique; Section 2 makes the prior art on each explicit. By taking the compliance-relevant decision—threshold evaluation and route update—out of the cloud critical path, the fog tier allows a graduated enforcement engine and a citizen gamification layer to be coupled end-to-end. Every headline figure goes back to a seeded script (Table 1). Namely:

Summary of contributions and their validation status.

  • A three-tier architecture with a measured case for the split: edge bins, district fog nodes, and a cloud analytics tier, with a reproducible component-budget model (Section 4.5) estimating 30.9 ms against 233.1 ms for an otherwise identical alert.

  • Multi-parameter edge sensing (fill level, methane, temperature, and weight) exercised on a simulated 120-bin, 20-city dataset (Section 4.4) whose distributional properties and missingness are reported rather than assumed.

  • A routing choice justified by benchmark, not asserted: greedy nearest-neighbor is fast but carries a 21.4% gap to the proven optimum, while adding 2-opt reaches 5.1% at sub-millisecond cost, matching tuned metaheuristics costing two to three orders of magnitude more compute (Section 5.3).

  • A policy-compliance engine (three-warning buffer, automated fines, paid-disposal mode, and Eco-Score) labeled consistently as a simulated prototype, not a field-validated intervention (Section 5.9).

  • Scalability and fault-robustness characterization to 20,000 bins, quantifying fog-tier mitigation under four sensor failure modes rather than assuming it (Sections 5.5, 5.6).

  • A governance and regulatory analysis of the instrument, not only the artifact: we identify the governance problems the system addresses (Section 1.1) and place the enforcement design within two literatures, responsive regulation and policy instruments (Section 2.4). We then lay out the regulatory difficulties a deployment would face—legal authority for automated penalties, technological due process, the automation of administrative discretion, attribution in communal infrastructure, distributive incidence, procedural legitimacy, data protection, and institutional capacity—together with the mitigations each demands (Section 7). By using our own fault-injection findings to bound the wrongful-penalty rate the design would impose, we convert an abstract due-process concern into a quantity that a regulator can set a threshold on.

1.3 Paper organization

Section 2 reviews the related work and positions this article against the 2024–2026 literature through a comparison table, including a review of the public-governance, policy-instrument, and regulatory-governance literatures in Section 2.4. Section 3 contains a notation table and presents the architecture and formulation. Section 4 describes implementation, data source, and simulation configuration. Results appear in Section 5. Section 7 analyses the regulatory and policy challenges a deployment would face. Section 8 concludes, and Section 9 sets out limitations and future work.

2 Related work

2.1 IoT and multi-parameter sensing

Early smart bins had ultrasonic fill-level sensing and basic cloud telemetry (Gutierrez et al., 2015), and Anagnostopoulos et al. (2015) added GPS-based fleet tracking on a cloud-centric pipeline. Recent multi-sensor deployments have closed much of the gap this article might otherwise have claimed. Mehta et al. (2025) tested ESP8266 bins with ultrasonic, MQ-4 methane, MQ-136 H2S, and MQ-137 NH3 sensors and GPS in Malad, Mumbai, validating readings against a Testo 340 analyzer at 96–97% agreement and reporting a greedy dynamic-CVRP routing layer with statistically validated results (paired t = 4.73, p = 0.0012). We cite this prior art rather than elide it, as it is nearest to our sensing and routing halves. Alsayaydeh et al. (2025) performed a five-sensor retrofit with a 30-day, 12-bin municipal trial and GPS-guided routing. Alnanih et al. (2025) and Bou-Rabee et al. (2025) contributed software-engineering-integrated monitoring and a battery-free design, respectively, both lacking a fog tier. Chen et al. (2025) performed waste-type recognition through audio and RGB feature fusion, while Da Silva and González (2025) and Henaien et al. (2024) performed more general multi-parameter capture. Kumar et al. (2025) extend the AI-IoT paradigm to hazardous hospital waste, combining real-time monitoring with machine-learning classification for segregation and compliance tracking. It is therefore evident that integrating sensing, policy enforcement, and sustainability objectives in one architecture has value—the principle we apply to the municipal context. None of the above places a fog tier between bins and cloud, and none couples sensing to compliance enforcement; both are what we add, not what we invent.

2.2 Fog computing and edge analytics

Bonomi et al. (2012) proposed fog computing as latency-reducing middleware for smart-city IoT; Aazam and Huh (2016) showed fog-cloud cooperation filters 40–70% of telemetry redundancy before the cloud; and Mahmud et al. (2018) studied module-placement policies motivating the offload of latency-sensitive logic to intermediate nodes. Recent work sharpens this: Sfaxi et al. (2024) propose a proactive latency-aware placement policy, Hossam et al. (2024) benchmark energy-aware placement in iFogSim against cloud-only and latency-aware baselines—the protocol we mirror in Section 4.5—and Hassan and Mehmood (2025) evaluate a multi-tier edge-fog framework in iFogSim2, noting simplified topological simulation as a limitation. We take the same care: our main latency number sits within an analytical component-budget model with Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation, which we have cross-checked against a discrete-event iFogSim run of the same topology (Section 5.2) that agrees within the model's sensitivity band. Hardware parameterization (MIPS, RAM, and bandwidth) follows iFogSim (Gupta et al., 2017), still the reference toolkit.

2.3 Dynamic routing and logistics heuristics

Waste collection routing is a version of the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). Kim et al. (2014) utilize adaptive large neighborhood search, while Buhrkal et al. (2012) and Ghahramani et al. (2022) claim that greedy nearest-neighbor heuristics refreshed from live sensor triggers are competitive at far lower cost than exact or metaheuristic solvers—a claim we do not accept and test directly (Section 5.3). The 2024–2025 literature has shifted to learned and hybrid solvers: Wang H. et al. (2025) improved an ant-colony algorithm for MSW transport in an Internet-of-Vehicles setting, Zhao et al. (2024) combined Q-learning hyperheuristics with particle swarm optimization for energy-aware dynamic routing, Khallaf et al. (2025) with several CEVRP papers (Wang C. et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) applied deep reinforcement learning to capacitated routing more broadly, and Sepúlveda-Campos et al. (2025) provided a fill-level-dependent service-time formulation more rigorous than threshold-triggered dispatch. A study that advocates plain greedy nearest-neighbor alone makes a case against a stronger field than it recognizes, which is why Section 5.3 benchmarks ours directly against this landscape—2-opt, a genetic algorithm, ant colony optimization, and particle swarm optimization on the same instances.

2.4 Public governance, policy instruments, and regulatory governance

The smart-waste systems literature has developed largely in isolation from the public-governance literature, and the omission is as much ours as the field's. This subsection outlines the work bearing on an architecture whose output is a penalty, an incentive, and a service obligation.

2.4.1 Regulatory governance and enforcement design

Baldwin et al. (2012) give the standard account of regulatory strategy and instrument selection, and Hood et al. (2001) show that regulatory regimes are shaped less by the objective size of a risk than by the information and institutional context around it—directly relevant to a system whose principal claim is to supply information previously absent. The responsive regulation of Ayres and Braithwaite (1992) supplies the enforcement pyramid that our warning-then-fine buffer instantiates: because starting at the top of the pyramid provokes resistance, sanctions escalate only as cooperation fails. Bardach and Kagan (1982) document that resistance empirically as “regulatory unreasonableness.” Black and Baldwin (2010) argue that risk-based regulation must account for regulators' limited attention and changing behavior, and Sparrow (2000) points out that effective regulation proceeds problem-by-problem on measured risk concentrations rather than by uniform inspection. Both describe what telemetry-driven targeting would enable, and both warn that a measurement system determines which problems become visible and hence which get addressed. Gunningham et al. (1998) argue for complementary instrument mixes in environmental policy rather than single instruments, the position our combined incentive-plus-sanction design adopts. On why people comply at all, May (2004) distinguishes affirmative from deterrence-based motivations, and Tyler (2006) shows that perceived procedural fairness predicts compliance more reliably than expected penalties—a finding with sharp implications for an automated fine (Section 7).

2.4.2 Policy instruments and policy design

Hood and Margetts (2007) classify the government's tools by the resources they draw on: nodality, authority, treasure, and organization. Our system is unusual in engaging all four at once, being a detector (nodality), a penalty (authority), a fee and reward scheme (treasure), and a dispatch system (organization). Howlett (2019) treats the choice and calibration of instruments as a design problem with its own failure modes, notably incoherent instrument mixes. Dunleavy et al. (2006) characterize digital-era governance as reintegration and needs-based holism facilitated by digitization, which is a fair description of what a three-tier municipal stack attempts.

2.4.3 Administrative discretion and algorithmic regulation

According to Lipsky (2010), policy is effectively made by street-level officials exercising discretion under scarcity, not by the statute alone. Bovens and Zouridis (2002) illustrate how information systems convert street-level bureaucracies into system-level bureaucracies: discretion therefore migrates from the officer to the system designer, with consequences for constitutional control. Peeters and Widlak (2018) describe the resulting structure as a “digital cage,” in which citizens cannot correct the records that determine how they are treated. The basics of technological due process are set out by Citron (2008): notice, reasons, auditability, and a genuine opportunity to contest. Coglianese and Lehr (2017) examine when automated decisions can lawfully carry administrative authority at all. Yeung (2018) provides an important critical account of algorithmic regulation, and the companion analysis of “hypernudge”. Yeung (2017) describes exactly the mechanism of a continuously updated behavioral score such as our Eco-Score. Veale and Brass (2019), Janssen and Kuk (2016), and Binns (2018) address, respectively, public-sector machine learning in practice, the limits of technocratic data-driven governance, and what algorithmic accountability requires of public reason.

2.4.4 Smart-city governance and its critics

Meijer and Bolívar (2016) study smart urban governance and find that most “smart city” claims emphasize technology rather than governance arrangements. Kitchin (2016) sets out the ethical and political questions urban data systems raise; Vanolo (2014) argues that smart-city discourse operates as a disciplinary technology that relocates responsibility onto citizens; and Cardullo and Kitchin (2019) show empirically how thin “smart citizen” participation typically is—a caution we apply directly to our own gamification layer. On data protection specifically, Edwards (2016) and Van Zoonen (2016) examine why smart-city telemetry resists conventional privacy governance.

2.4.5 Waste governance and the informal sector

Kaza et al. (2018) and Guerrero et al. (2013) establish that institutional and financial arrangements, rather than technology, dominate waste-management outcomes in developing cities. For India specifically, Doron and Jeffrey (2018) and Mani and Singh (2016) describe the policy landscape in which the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India, 2016) operate. Critically for an enforcement system, Demaria and Schindler (2016), Gidwani (2015) and Gutberlet (2015) document that a large share of actual recycling labor is performed by informal workers whose livelihoods a formalized, penalty-bearing system can displace rather than support; Eubanks (2018) provides the general case that automated administrative systems tend to fall hardest on the poor.

2.4.6 What is missing

The smart-waste systems we reviewed in Sections 2.1–2.3 do not engage this literature, and the governance literature in turn rarely engages the architectural choices—where a decision is computed, with what latency, and with what error rate—that determine whether a governance mechanism is administrable at all. We link the two together: Section 7 interprets the quantitative properties measured in Section 5 as regulatory parameters.

2.5 Digital governance and gamification

Botsman and Rogers (2010) research sharing-economy incentive dashboards, and Thaler and Sunstein's nudge theory Thaler and Sunstein, (2008) motivates positive-reinforcement compliance. Our prototype does not clear the empirical bar set by recent gamified-recycling studies: Venturi et al. (2025) divide 26 participants across paper, app, and gamified-app conditions; Rosenlund et al. (2025) field-test a gamified recycling station with 15 households; and Saeedi (2024) designs a blockchain loyalty program structurally close to our Eco-Score. Our three-warning-then-fine buffer is structurally a graduated Pay-As-You-Throw tariff, and PAYT has a mature econometric literature we had not engaged: Rizzo and Secomandi (2024) study threshold tariffs directly, Compagnoni and Torbert (2026) provide a difference-in-differences causal evaluation, and Ghimire et al. (2024) study willingness-to-pay in Kathmandu, bearing on whether INR fines of our magnitude are realistic here. None of them legitimizes our particular fine schedule or Eco-Score curve, which is why we do not present our policy numbers as validated behavioral results (Section 5.9).

2.6 Comparison table and identified research gaps

Table 2 summarizes a dozen of the most directly comparable systems across six capability axes. To our knowledge, nothing in the wider literature combines a fog or edge compute tier with multi-parameter sensing, dynamic routing, graduated compliance enforcement, and citizen gamification in one pipeline, and this article closes that vertical-integration gap. We do not claim algorithmic novelty: as Sections 2.1–2.4 make clear, the individual sensing, fog-placement, and routing techniques all have closer and often more rigorously validated prior art, and our benchmark (Section 5.3) shows plain greedy nearest-neighbor is measurably weaker than several alternatives.

Table 2 identifies four gaps. First, no reviewed system couples fog-tier alert evaluation to policy enforcement: compliance logic is either absent or built on a cloud-only pipeline. Second, we located no system combining citizen-facing gamification with automated fining; the econometric PAYT literature and the gamification literature remain separate. Third, few end-to-end efforts connect fog-tier simulation metrics (latency, energy) with municipal application-layer KPIs (compliance rate, dispatch cost). Fourth, and cutting across the other three, none of the reviewed systems engages the regulatory-governance literature on enforcement design, administrative due process, or instrument choice (Section 2.4), even where—as with Mehta et al. (2025) and Kumar et al. (2025)—the system issues or supports compliance decisions. Systems that impose consequences on identifiable people are policy instruments, and the literature on designing such instruments is not an optional context. This article seeks to fill exactly these four gaps, while using rather than replacing the routing and sensing techniques of earlier work.

3.2 Three-tier architecture design

The architecture (Figure 1) allows thousands of bins to report telemetry without stressing the local network or bottlenecking on cloud ingress. Logic is divided across three tiers.

Figure 1

  • Edge tier (smart bins): a microcontroller along with four sensors, namely ultrasonic for fill level, MQ-4 for methane, a load cell for weight, and a thermistor/DS18B20 for temperature, performing sampling, plausibility filtering, and timestamping before transmission.

  • Fog tier (district nodes): a gateway of Raspberry Pi 4B class (2,800 MIPS, 4 GB RAM) takes in edge streams over a low-latency WLAN link and carries out threshold evaluation and route recomputation. This tier determines the alert-to-actuation latency budget (Section 4.5) and runs independently of the cloud round-trip for that reason.

  • Cloud tier (global analytics): the compliance engine, longitudinal master records and city-wide gamification aggregation run on a shared 44,800 MIPS analytics server. It is a layer that tolerates hundreds of milliseconds of latency and benefits from a centralized state.

3.3 Sensor state vector and application DAG

At a point in time t, edge node i records the state vector (Equation 1) in which

in which Fi is the fill level in percent, Mi the methane concentration in ppm, Ti the ambient temperature in degrees Celsius and Wi the waste weight in kg. The raw streams FILL_DATA, METHANE_DATA, TEMP_DATA, and WEIGHT_DATA are treated as a distributed application DAG with tuple selectivity 0.25 across the four concurrent streams; each cycle aggregates them into a single SENSOR_AGGREGATE tuple before it leaves the edge tier.

3.4 Threshold policies and fine formulation

The government has set operating limits of F ≤ 85, M ≤ 400, 0 ≤ T ≤ 50, and W ≤ 500. Any event exceeding these triggers an automatic fine (INR):

in which the thermal-hazard term (Equation 3) captures unusually high fire or freezing risk:

To avoid punishing isolated violations or those caused by sensor noise, the cloud tier applies a rolling monthly warning buffer. Let vu, m be the number of violation events attributed to user u in month m; the fine that then applies (Equation 4) is

This buffer is akin to a graduated Pay-As-You-Throw tariff (cf. Rizzo and Secomandi, 2024; Compagnoni and Torbert, 2026). We discuss the similarities, along with the absence of field validation for the specific INR thresholds used, in Section 5.9.

3.5 Gamification and longitudinal eco-score

A citizen's Eco-Score Su (Equation 5) is formed from their compliance history and their cumulative carbon impact:

in which CCO2 denotes the citizen's cumulative CO2-equivalent impact (Table 4) and α, β are weights defined by the system; the municipal reward pool is tiered by score grade, from A+ down to D. The prototype exercises the mechanism under simulated citizen-behavior traces, without validation against real behavior; Section 5.9 explains why we do not report an observed Eco-Score trajectory as an empirical result.

3.6 Predictive routing and optimization

A bin is marked urgent when Fi≥85%. For non-urgent bins, the estimated time-to-fill τi (hours) (Equation 6) is

in which ρi denotes the bin's historic fill rate (%/hour). A bin enters the active dispatch queue when τi < 24 hours or after a hazard threshold has been breached.

Inter-bin distance uses the Haversine great-circle formula (Equations 7 and 8), since planar Euclidean distance is not an adequate approximation at the municipal scale:

with ϕ the latitude, λ the longitude and r = 6371 km. The fog tier generates its initial tour by greedy nearest-neighbor over urgency-prioritized bins and then applies a 2-opt local search pass. This is the right point on the quality/latency trade-off for a resource-constrained node: Section 5.3 shows that 2-opt closes about 16 of greedy's 21.4 percentage-point gap to the proven optimum for 0.67 ms per route, and matches tuned ant colony optimization at roughly 1, 670 × less compute. As new telemetry arrives, routes are recomputed every fog processing cycle.

4 Implementation details

The system has two evaluation surfaces. The first is a functional application stack (Flask/SQLAlchemy backend, PostgreSQL cloud store, SQLite fog cache, HTML5/Chart.js dashboard) exercising the full sensing-to-policy pipeline. The second is the set of stand-alone seeded Python experiments in experiments/, which yield every quantitative claim in Section 5. Since each script is independently re-runnable and writes its parameters and results into a JSON artifact, reproducibility is built in rather than asserted.

4.1 Technology stack and data models

The backend is built on Python 3.9 with Flask and SQLAlchemy. District fog nodes hold a SQLite cache for low-latency threshold checks, while the cloud tier uses PostgreSQL for gamification state, longitudinal records, and historical analytics. Fleet mapping and metric visualization use HTML5/CSS3 and Chart.js. The normalized schema is presented in Table 5.

4.3 Policy engine and feature deployment

The cloud application layer encodes the mechanisms of Section 3. A three-warning buffer checks vu, m per household and waives the fine for the first three monthly violations with only a small Eco-Score penalty. Automated fining works from the parameters of Equation 2, charging INR 10 per excess percentage point of fill and a flat INR 1000 for a high-temperature hazard. Paid-disposal mode applies a per-kg service price by real-time sensor band once a threshold warning is breached, and a gamified reward loop recomputes the Eco-Score after each disposal event, logging the change as a digital credit.

4.4 Dataset provenance and profile

The sensor dataset used throughout this study (smart-waste-collection-sensor-data.csv) is synthetically generated, not collected from physically deployed bins. It consists of 120 records from 20 Indian cities, with bin coordinates at actual landmarks but readings generated by data_simulator.py: six readings per bin, no duplicate IDs, timestamps spanning 2024-05-03 to 2024-06-19, and the distributional profile including missingness in Table 7. Every downstream experiment is calibrated against it: the routing benchmark (Section 5.3), scalability (Section 5.5), and fault injection (Section 5.6) all use synthetic coordinates drawn from its spatial density, with fill-rate and fault distributions set from its empirical mean and standard deviation.

4.4.1 Generation, preprocessing, and validation status

data_simulator.py (i) fixes 120 bin locations at named landmarks; (ii) assigns each bin a type and base fill rate; (iii) draws six timestamped readings per bin over a 47-day window from truncated Gaussians whose means and spreads follow municipal reference ranges, with fill uniform-to-saturation per bin type, temperature set to Indian-city seasonal norms and battery to a discharge curve; and (iv) drops each non-fill field independently with probability ≈0.05 to mimic radio and sensor dropout. Preprocessing is limited to type coercion, ISO-8601 timestamp parsing, range assertion against the bounds of Section 3, and per-field mean/SD extraction; no imputation, smoothing, or outlier removal is applied, and rows with missing fields are retained. Since the dataset is synthetic, it is not independently validated against a physical deployment, and no such validation is asserted. Calibration targets are drawn from ranges reported in the multi-parameter sensing literature (Mehta et al., 2025; Alsayaydeh et al., 2025; Henaien et al., 2024); in future work (Section 9), we plan to swap these for a field-collected trace and re-run every downstream experiment.

4.4.2 Sensor error model calibrated to real gas-sensor data

Although the bin dataset is synthetic, the sensor error model in the hazard-alert path is calibrated to real data. experiments/sensor_calibration.py processes the UCI “Gas sensor array under dynamic gas mixtures” dataset (Fonollosa et al., 2015) (a 16-channel metal-oxide array under dynamic methane/ethylene mixtures, ~12 h at 100 Hz), identifies the methane-responsive channels (|r|≈0.7 on ethylene-free windows), and estimates a measurement-noise SD of about 0.29% of full scale, baseline drift of about 0.32% per hour, response lag of about 1.05 s and a natural spike rate of about 0.06% of samples. These values replace the magnitudes previously assumed in Section 5.6; the injected rates of up to 50% are, by contrast, a deliberate adversarial stress test far above the natural rate.

The reported bin_status is normal (69), maintenance_required (27), full (20), and offline (4), while bin_type is general (47), hazardous (34), compost (22), and recycling (17). Figure 2 shows the fill-level and temperature distributions against the operating thresholds of Section 3, together with the status breakdown. Because the 120 bins span 20 cities, a single truck tour across all of them makes no physical sense. The routing and scalability experiments (Section 5) therefore sample a city centroid and generate service points around it using a realistic municipal service radius (σ≈0.045°≈5 km), preserving the spatial density of the dataset rather than its inter-city spread. The fill-rate and fault-injection distributions used in the simulations are matched to this dataset's empirical mean and standard deviation rather than to arbitrary constants.

4.5 Fog-tier latency model

Our primary latency estimate is a component-budget analytical model. experiments/latency_model.py uses the same MIPS and bandwidth values as Table 8, with a 5,000-replicate seeded Monte Carlo over the stochastic stages—sensor-acquisition timing and network jitter—while compute stages are deterministic given instruction-count and MIPS assumptions. We keep this as the main figure because parameter uncertainty propagates through it. It is validated by two independent discrete-event simulations: an executed iFogSim run of the topology SmartWasteManagementFog.java (compiled against iFogSim (Gupta et al., 2017) with the bundled CloudSim), and a custom SimPy queued model (experiments/latency_des.py) covering all four load scenarios. The three are compared in Table 9 of Section 5.2.

4.5.1 Distributional assumptions

Sensor acquisition is a deterministic function of bin depth, with depth ~ Normal (1.10 m, 0.08 m) clipped to [0.4, 2.0] m and mapped through ultrasonic round-trip physics, reflecting standard 240 L municipal bin dimensions. Edge-to-fog jitter is Normal (6.0, 2.5) ms clipped at 0.5 ms, from published WLAN measurements in IoT gateway configurations (Aazam and Huh, 2016); fog-to-actuator dispatch is Normal(18.0, 6.0) ms clipped at 1.0 ms, from REST push relay latency to truck-mounted displays; and the counterfactual fog-to-cloud WAN is Normal (100.0, 22.0) ms clipped at 10.0 ms, matching the iFogSim topology's stated uplink. The four stochastic stages are considered mutually independent, because each depends on an unrelated physical mechanism—bin geometry, local WLAN contention, the REST relay path, and the wide-area link, respectively—although correlated network congestion could introduce dependencies in a real deployment.

4.5.2 Sensitivity analysis

Adjusting each parameter individually by ±25% leaves the fog-mediated path within 24.7–38.2 ms (baseline 30.9 ms), with fog-to-actuator dispatch the most influential parameter, accounting for 78% of the variance. No perturbation brings the fog path near the 500 ms actuation budget.

4.6 Simulation topology

The iFogSim topology (ifogsim_simulation/SmartWasteManagementFog.java) describes a 44,800 MIPS/40 GB cloud tier, a 2,800 MIPS/4 GB fog tier on a 100 ms uplink, and 1,000 MIPS/1 GB edge bins on a 2 ms uplink, configured with 20, 30, 50 and 80 bins for the latency, balanced, stress and energy scenarios (Table 8). It was compiled against iFogSim/CloudSim and executed for the latency scenario, the loop-delay result being reported as a discrete-event cross-check in Section 5.2. Its bandwidth and latency values are exactly those feeding the analytical model of Section 4.5.

4.7 Statistical methods

Every inferential statistic follows one protocol. Each experiment fixes a unit of replication: a generated routing instance, a paired static/dynamic 28-day run, a fault-rate run, or a repeated timing of one bin count. Replicate counts are chosen so the 95% confidence half-width on the primary metric is below 5% of its mean—n = 30 for the routing, dispatch, and fault studies, n = 3 per size for scalability, where run-to-run variance is small (CV < 2%). Reported intervals are 95% confidence intervals, with a bias-corrected bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples) additionally given for the dispatch saving. The dispatch comparison is paired on the same demand realization, so we use a paired t-test, apply the Shapiro–Wilk test to the paired differences to check normality (W = 0.967, p = 0.42), and use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test as a distribution-free confirmation; the effect size is Cohen's d for paired samples. The scalability exponent is obtained by ordinary least squares regression of log(time) against logn, with SE and CI taken from the regression. We apply no multiple-comparison correction, since each experiment tests one pre-specified primary hypothesis, and all p-values are two-sided.

4.7.1 No physical hardware prototype has been deployed, and no field-collected sensor data exists

As every dataset is synthetic, these statistics measure how much the simulation varies under reseeding, not the sampling uncertainty one would see for a real population; practical significance is discussed alongside magnitude in Section 6.

5 Results

5.1 Provenance and status of the results

No physical hardware prototype has been deployed, and no field-collected sensor data exists. Every quantitative result below comes from seeded computational experiments: an analytical component-budget latency model (Section 5.2), a routing solver benchmark on synthetic bin coordinates (Section 5.3), a service-parity dispatch comparison (Section 5.4), wall-clock scalability measurements (Section 5.5), and a sensor fault-injection simulation (Section 5.6). Hardware parameters (Table 8) come from manufacturers' datasheets and published specifications, not measured devices, and the sensor dataset itself (Section 4.4) is synthetic.

Table 10 makes the epistemic status of every headline number explicit, classifying each as analytical (closed-form or component-budget model), Monte Carlo (stochastic simulation with seeded replicates), or wall-clock (measured execution time of our own code on commodity hardware). No entry is an experimental measurement of a physical deployment. The 30.9 ms alert-path latency is an output of the analytical model of Section 4.5, not a packet-timing measurement, and the fuel, CO2, and cost figures of Section 5.8 are estimates conditional on the assumptions stated there, not observed savings.

5.2 End-to-end latency

According to the analytical model of Section 4.5, the fog-mediated alert path has a latency of 30.9 ms (95% CI 30.7–31.1 ms; n = 5, 000 replicates), against 233.1 ms (95% CI 231.8–234.3 ms) for the same alert routed through the cloud—an 86.8% reduction, inside the 500 ms actuation budget in 100% of replicates (Figure 3). Most of the time goes on the fog-to-actuator dispatch step (mean 18.0 ms) rather than compute: edge and fog compute stages are both sub-0.1 ms at the stated MIPS budgets, so the practical floor is set by network and sensor-acquisition physics rather than processing power. This also resolves an inconsistency in the architecture as originally described, where a “Cloud Auth” stage dominated the reported breakdown even though threshold evaluation was said to happen at the fog tier precisely to avoid a cloud round trip; the revised model keeps the cloud off the critical path, consistent with the stated design.

Figure 3

5.2.1 Two independent discrete-event cross-checks

This analytical figure is confirmed by two distinct discrete-event simulations (Table 9). First, the iFogSim topology (SmartWasteManagementFog.java, compiled against iFogSim/CloudSim) was run for the latency-test scenario with 20 bins. Its fog-mediated sensor-to-actuator loop— FILL_DATA→client_module→fog_module→client_module→TRUCK_ACTUATOR, cloud off the loop—reports a mean loop delay of 23.3 ms, and tuple-level fog compute of 0.03–0.34 ms confirms compute is not the bottleneck. Second, a purpose-built SimPy model with explicit FIFO queues at the fog and cloud tiers, link serialization, and stochastic sensor timing was run across all four load scenarios (20–80 bins, 2–10 s intervals, >104 alert cycles each). It gives a fog-mediated loop delay of 29.3 ms (P95 38.4 ms, P99 43.5 ms) against a 235 ms cloud counterfactual, stable across every load: fog-tier utilization stays below 1%, so no queueing regime is entered, and 100% of alert cycles finish inside the 500 ms budget. The three methods (analytical 30.9 ms, iFogSim 23.3 ms, SimPy DES 29.3 ms) agree to within the analytical model's ±25% sensitivity band. Artifacts: ifogsim_simulation/results/ and experiments/results/latency_des.json.

5.3 Routing algorithm comparison

5.3.1 Problem formulation

Every benchmark instance is a single-vehicle open-tour routing problem over the bins whose dispatch predicate fired in one fog cycle (Section 3.6): bin i is included when Fi≥85% or τi < 24 h. Given the included set B with Haversine great-circle distances dij and a fixed depot b0 at the city centroid, a solver returns a permutation π of B minimizing from b0. The tour is open, with no forced return leg, since trucks continue to the disposal facility. The benchmark focuses on the sequencing sub-problem: instances are sized to one truck-load, so the 35-stop capacity constraint—matched to the 240 L-bin × compactor-volume ratio of Section 5.4—is not binding within an instance. Multi-vehicle assignment and capacity triage are handled upstream by the fullest-first queue of Section 5.4, not by the solver under test, and time windows and traffic are out of scope (Section 9). The instances are 30 independent replicates of 40 bins each, with coordinates from the city-centroid spatial model of Section 4.4 (σ≈0.045°) and NumPy PRNG seed 42.

5.3.2 Reference solver and metaheuristic tuning

The reference is a proven optimum, not a heuristic bound. routing_exact_and_tuning.py solves each 41-node instance to optimality with a Dantzig–Fulkerson–Johnson mixed-integer formulation, branch-and-cut in CBC, and lazy subtour-elimination cuts added until the relaxation returns a single tour. All 30 evaluation instances and the 10 held-out tuning instances achieved proven optimality (Optimal status, mean solve time 0.36 s), with optimal tours averaging 103.5 km (95% CI 100.7–107.1 km), so every gap below is a true optimality gap. To eliminate any perception that the GA/ACO/PSO figures reflect untuned defaults, each metaheuristic's parameters were chosen by random search (16 configurations per solver) on the 10 held-out instances (seeds 900–909, disjoint from evaluation), scored by mean optimality gap and locked before evaluation. The tuned configurations are given in Table 11.

We benchmark six practical solvers against the exact optimum—greedy nearest-neighbor, greedy+2-opt, Clarke–Wright savings, and tuned genetic, ant colony, and discrete particle swarm algorithms—across the 30 instances described above.

Table 12 and Figure 4 give the results. Plain greedy nearest-neighbor runs in 0.05 ms, but its tour is 21.4% longer than the proven optimum. A 2-opt pass reduces the gap to 5.1% (95% CI 4.2–6.1%) at 0.72 ms, reclaiming roughly 16 of those points for 0.67 ms of added compute. Tuned ant colony optimization reaches 4.2% (95% CI 3.2–5.1%), statistically indistinguishable from greedy+2-opt since the intervals overlap, but costs 1,205 ms per route—roughly 1,670 × more latency for no reliable quality gain at fog-node budgets. Tuning does not rescue the population methods: the tuned genetic algorithm trails at 12.0% for 1,141 ms and tuned particle swarm at 13.3% for 171 ms, both worse than greedy+2-opt on either axis. Clarke–Wright performs worst at 72.7%, consistent with its depot-radial construction bias. We therefore adopt greedy+2-opt as the fog-tier default, since it matches the best metaheuristic quality we could obtain at three orders of magnitude less compute.

5.4 Dynamic dispatch vs. static schedule: service-parity comparison

Testing dynamic dispatch against one fixed cadence is not meaningful: a slow cadence looks cheap but overflows constantly, a fast one looks wasteful, so either choice lets the comparison be tuned to the desired conclusion. We instead sweep the static cadence over 1–4 day intervals to trace the cost/service frontier (Figure 5) and report the saving against the cheapest static cadence whose overflow rate matches the dynamic policy's—the only comparison that isolates telemetry-driven bin selection from simply collecting more often. Both policies share route construction (greedy+2-opt) and differ only in bin selection, over a rolling 28-day horizon with a 35-stop capacity limit and fullest-first triage. The dynamic policy forecasts fill from a noisy rate estimate (coefficient of variation 0.30) rather than from ground truth, so its advantage cannot stem from oracle knowledge.

Figure 5

At matched service level—a 1-day static cadence giving 16.1 mean overflow events per 28-day period against the dynamic policy's 16.4—dynamic dispatch cuts mean daily travel from 102.67 to 63.81 km, a 37.9% reduction (95% CI [34.8%, 41.0%]; paired t = 24.97, p = 3.7 × 10−21; Wilcoxon p = 1.9 × 10−9; Cohen's d = 4.01; Shapiro–Wilk W = 0.967, p = 0.42; bootstrap 95% CI [35.1%, 40.8%], 10,000 resamples; n = 30). Mean daily stops fall from 35.0 to 15.2, a 56.6% reduction (95% CI [52.1%, 61.1%]), because only the bins that need it are visited. The paired differences have mean Δ = 38.86 km/day, SD = 8.49 and median = 38.2.

5.4.1 Validation on a real road network

To rule out the saving being an artifact of straight-line distance, we re-ran the identical comparison with the Haversine matrix replaced by shortest-path distance on the OpenStreetMap drivable street graph of a Chennai municipal zone (Ambattur/Anna Nagar, 5 km radius, 20,212 nodes, 51,190 edges; experiments/routing_real_roads.py) retrieved with OSMnx (Boeing, 2017), snapping bins to the nearest street node. The measured circuity factor is 1.33, normal for dense Indian street grids. On the real network the saving is 38.7% (95% CI [33.8%, 43.5%], n = 24 of 30 replicates; in six, no static cadence matched the dynamic policy's service level), statistically indistinguishable from the Haversine figure on the same instances (35.8%), and greedy+2-opt's optimality gap in fact improves (2.3% against 5.5%) because the street topology removes many tour crossings that a 2-opt pass would otherwise fix. The headline saving is therefore robust to the distance metric.

5.5 Scalability

Route computation uses on-demand Haversine evaluation rather than a materialized n×n distance matrix, which at n = 10, 000 would need 800 MB and exceed a 4 GB fog node's working budget once OS and runtime overhead are counted. All scalability measurements were performed on a single core, normalized to Raspberry Pi 4B-class throughput (2,800 MIPS, 4 GB RAM). For each bin count n∈{100, 250, 500, 1000, 2, 500, 5, 000, 10, 000, 20, 000}, bins were sampled around a city centroid within a realistic municipal service radius (σ≈0.045°≈5 km). This preserves the spatial density of the 120-bin dataset (Section 4.4) at roughly 150 bins per 10 km × 10 km area, with three repetitions per size at different seeds.

Measured wall-clock time scales as O(n1.72) (R2 = 0.995, regression p = 4.9 × 10−8), sub-quadratic in practice thanks to vectorized distance evaluation, against a theoretical O(n2) worst case for greedy nearest-neighbor. The fitted exponent is 1.72 (SE = 0.052), giving a 95% CI of [1.62, 1.83]. At n = 10, 000, route computation takes 1,335 ms and at n = 20, 000, 5,235 ms (Figure 6), with peak on-demand memory of 0.48 MB against 3,200 MB for a materialized matrix. Extrapolation beyondn = 20, 000should be treated cautiously, since the fit may not hold where memory-hierarchy effects dominate. Beyond single-node capacity, bins are sharded across district fog nodes, and the per-node cost scales as O((n/k)2) for k districts. Single-node performance therefore degrades gracefully to that scale, and sharding is the intended mitigation beyond it rather than an untested assumption.

Figure 6

5.6 Sensor fault robustness

Across 200 simulated bins, 30 replicates per rate from 0 to 50%, we inject four failure modes from the field-deployment literature—dropout (battery or radio loss), stuck-at (firmware hang), drift (calibration or thermal aging) and spike (EMI or condensation)—and compare overflow-alert F1 with and without a fog-tier mitigation filter performing physical-bounds rejection, staleness detection and prediction fallback from the historic rate. Table 13 and Figure 7 show mitigation improves F1 at every non-zero fault rate, the gap widening as faults become more common: from 0.970 → 0.979 at 5% to 0.696 → 0.797 at 50%. This gives a measured degradation curve for sensor-failure handling rather than an assumption of sensor reliability.

Sensor fault analysis: F1, missed alerts (false negatives), and false alerts (false positives), with and without fog-tier mitigation (30 replicates per rate, 200 bins, all four failure modes pooled).

5.6.1 Robustness to calibrated fault magnitudes

Re-running the study with drift and noise magnitudes calibrated to the UCI gas-sensor dataset (Section 4.4; drift SD 27%-fill over a 7-day recalibration interval, a measurement-noise floor of 0.29%-fill on every reading; experiments/fault_injection_calibrated.py) gives the same conclusion: the fog-tier mitigation still improves F1 at every non-zero fault rate, from 0.955 → 0.969 at 5% to 0.684 → 0.784 at 50%. The assumed fault magnitudes, therefore, do not account for the mitigation benefit.

5.6.2 False-negative and false-positive analysis

Missed-alert and false-alert counts convey the asymmetric safety implications: a missed methane breach could allow toxic gas to accumulate, whereas a false alert triggers an unnecessary dispatch. The mitigation filter reduces missed alerts by 94–97% across all rates (8.70 to 1.20 at 50% faults), the most consequential improvement for safety, while false alerts rise slightly (15.13 to 16.43) because prediction fallback occasionally fires on historical fill-rate estimates when a reading is anomalous but within bounds. By mode, dropout and stuck-at chiefly cause missed alerts, since sensor silence reads as “no problem,” while drift and spike chiefly cause false alerts. The filter is accordingly most effective against dropout and stuck-at, and least effective against gradual drift, which stays within physical bounds while being factually wrong.

5.7 Deployment cost

At pilot-volume retail pricing, a per-bin bill of materials (ESP32-WROOM-32, HC-SR04P ultrasonic, MQ-4 methane, DS18B20, 50 kg load cell with HX711, 18650 cell with BMS, solar panel, IP65 enclosure, NB-IoT/LoRa radio and assembly) gives a CAPEX of INR 3,160 (USD 37.62), with municipal tender pricing typically 30–40% lower. Adding a five-year amortized share of a district Raspberry Pi 4B gateway serving 250 bins, consistent with Section 5.5, plus annual connectivity and maintenance opex, gives a 5-year total cost of ownership of INR 6,493 per bin—itemized and currency-explicit rather than an unstated assumption of affordability.

5.8 Sustainability impact

The figures in this section are model-based estimates, not measured real-world savings, and every input assumption is stated so the estimate can be recomputed or contested. They come from the simulated routing saving of Section 5.4 (38.86 km/day/route) rather than being assumed independently, using IPCC 2006 Guidelines (Vol. 2, Ch. 3) diesel emission factors and BS-VI heavy-duty limits. Spread across a modeled 12-route municipal fleet, the estimate gives ≈170,222 km/year saved, ≈59,578 liters of diesel avoided, ≈159.67 tonnes of CO2-equivalent avoided and ≈INR 5,481,136/year in fuel cost avoided. Carrying the [34.8%, 41.0%] confidence interval through gives roughly ±8% on each figure, before further unquantified uncertainty in the emission factor, fuel price, and fleet size. The 12-route figure is a stated scaling choice, not a measured fleet size. Actual savings depend on real road distances, traffic, vehicle mix, driver behavior, and load factors, none modeled here; these should be read as an order-of-magnitude upper estimate pending the GPS-tracked field study of Section 9.2. They also support UN SDG 11 and SDG 13 as the relevant policy framing.

5.9 Policy layer: simulated, not field-validated

The prototype exercises the warning buffer, automated fining, paid-disposal mode, and Eco-Score gamification against synthetic citizen-behavior traces. The policy and gamification layer is a software prototype, not a field-validated behavioral intervention. We report it as an implementation-feasibility demonstration—that warning buffer, fine calculation, paid-disposal transition, and Eco-Score computation integrate architecturally with the sensing and routing pipeline—not as evidence of behavioral change or policy effectiveness.

5.9.1 Socio-technical considerations

Generating automated fines from sensor readings raises questions of fairness, due process, privacy, legitimacy, and distributive incidence that a production deployment must resolve. As these are regulatory and policy constraints rather than implementation details, we treat them in Section 7: appeal and due process in Section 7.2, fairness, income-sensitivity and informal-sector displacement in Section 7.5, behavioral acceptance and the legitimacy of the Eco-Score in Section 7.6, and data protection in Section 7.7. Table 14 states what each would require before deployment, and none of it is implemented in the prototype.
