Regulatory and policy challenges, where each arises in this system, and what a deployment would require.

“Evidence here” indicates where this article supplies a relevant quantity; it does not indicate that the challenge is resolved.

One issue belongs here rather than there, because it concerns the evaluation rather than the policy. The evaluation presumes trusted sensors and links; a deployment cannot. Relevant threats include spoofed or replayed telemetry used to induce wrongful fines or suppress genuine hazard alerts, tampering with a bin's own sensor to evade charges, denial-of-service against a district fog node, which would stall threshold evaluation and routing for a whole district, and compromise of the fine and Eco-Score records. The minimum countermeasures are per-device authenticated keys with signed, nonce-protected messages; rate limiting and anomaly detection at the fog tier; graceful degradation to a conservative fixed schedule when a fog node is unreachable; an append-only audit log for every fine; and standard hardening of the REST surface. None of this is implemented, and none of the results in Section 5 would survive an adversary who can forge telemetry.

Every study we know of reporting real behavior change from a comparable mechanism—Venturi et al.'s 26-participant gamification study (Venturi et al., 2025), Rosenlund et al.'s 15-household field trial (Rosenlund et al., 2025), and Ghaffari et al.'s randomized controlled trial on household sorting (Ghaffari et al., 2026)—used a field deployment with human participants. Ours has not been piloted with real households, so any number describing citizen response is a property of the simulation's behavioral assumptions rather than of citizens. We treat this as a limitation (Section 9) rather than glossing over it, and identify a field pilot structured after (Rosenlund et al., 2025) as the necessary next step before any compliance claim can be made empirically.

6 Discussion

Three principal findings emerge from the computational experiments.

6.1 Fog-tier offloading is architecturally justified, not merely convenient

The 7.5 × latency reduction (Section 5.2) is not a marginal improvement: at the 500 ms actuation budget required for methane and fire-hazard response, the cloud-mediated path consumes 47% of the budget on a single alert cycle, leaving no margin for queueing under load. Fog placement is therefore a structural requirement for time-critical safety alerts, not an optimization preference.

6.2 The routing quality–latency trade-off favors simple heuristics with local search

Plain greedy nearest-neighbor, the default in much of the prior waste-routing literature, carries a 21.4% gap to the proven optimum that the original manuscript did not disclose, and a single 2-opt pass closes about 16 of those points for 0.67 ms (Section 5.3). Given that tuned ant colony optimization is statistically indistinguishable in quality but costs ~1,670 × more compute, and that tuned GA and PSO are worse on both axes, fog-tier routing need not sacrifice quality for speed—but it does need to move beyond vanilla nearest-neighbor.

6.3 The policy layer is architecturally integrated but empirically unvalidated

The compliance and gamification pipeline shows that policy logic can coexist with operational routing in a single system, but every number describing citizen behavior is a property of the simulation's assumptions. Section 7 argues that the binding constraints on this component are, in any case, regulatory rather than technical, which makes it a hypothesis-generating prototype rather than a validated intervention.

6.4 Broader implications

For municipal authorities, this work lays down a reproducible computational baseline against which hardware prototypes and field pilots can be evaluated, with the seeded scripts and JSON artifacts providing transparent benchmarks for latency, routing quality, scalability, and fault tolerance rather than each paper constructing an ad-hoc evaluation setup. For the research community, benchmarking routing against a proven optimum supplies a reference comparison that prior work, typically benchmarked against a single baseline, has lacked.

7 Regulatory and policy challenges

Section 1.1 argued that the system is a policy instrument. Instruments that impose burdens on identifiable people are constrained in ways that optimizers are not, and those constraints are not deployment details to be resolved later: several of them determine whether the mechanism as designed is lawful and administrable at all. This section sets out the principal regulatory and policy challenges, and—where our own measurements bear on them—quantifies the constraint rather than merely naming it. Table 14 summarizes the analysis. We emphasize that this is a conceptual and literature-based analysis: no municipal legal review, administrative-law opinion, or consultation with an urban local body has been obtained (Section 9).

7.1 Legal authority and the delegation of penal decisions

A fine is an exercise of statutory power, and the first question a deploying authority faces is whether the power exists and whether a machine may exercise it. The Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Government of India, 2016) are specific on this point. Rule 15(zf) requires local authorities to “frame bye-laws and prescribe criteria for levying of spot fine for persons who litters or fails to comply with the provisions of these rules and delegate powers to officers or local bodies to levy spot fines as per the bye laws framed.” The penal power is therefore conferred by delegation on a named class of legal persons—officers, or local bodies—and the Rules envisage such an officer forming a view, not a threshold predicate firing. A sensor reading is evidence; the finding belongs to the officer. Automating the step from evidence to penalty, therefore, raises a familiar administrative-law question: whether a power delegated to an officer may be sub-delegated to an automated process, and whether doing so without express enabling provision is ultra vires. Coglianese and Lehr (2017) survey the conditions under which automated systems can carry administrative authority and conclude that the constraint is rarely technological; it is the presence of an accountable human decision-maker in the chain. The practical implication for this system is specific: the compliance engine should generate a proposed penalty with its supporting evidence package for ratification by an authorized officer, not an executed one. That is a change in the software's authority model, not merely in its user interface, and we did not implement it.

7.2 Technological due process and the wrongful-penalty rate

Where an automated decision is adverse to an individual, Citron's account of technological due process (Citron, 2008) requires at minimum notice of the decision and its basis, a statement of reasons, an audit trail sufficient to reconstruct the decision, and a real opportunity to contest it before an independent reviewer. These are all missing from the prototype (Section 5.9).

Our fault-injection findings quantify why this matters. At a 10% sensor-fault rate, the fog-tier mitigation filter still yields 3.17 false overflow alerts per 200 bins per evaluation cycle (Table 13), about 1.6 per 100 bins. If the same threshold-crossing logic were used to attribute a penalty, and the system were run daily across a 50,000-bin city, that corresponds to an order of 800 wrongful penalty events per day; at the 50% fault rate the figure is roughly 4,100. These are indicative rather than exact, because the fine predicate of Equation 2 spans four parameters while the fault study targets overflow alerts, and because a real deployment would presumably not run at a 50% fault rate. The point is structural: a non-zero sensor error rate is a non-zero wrongful-penalty rate, and it does not fall to zero as the filter improves. An appeals process is therefore not an optional citizen-experience feature but the mechanism by which the system's known error rate is reconciled with the requirement that penalties be correct. Treating it as an engineering quantity has a useful consequence: the tolerable wrongful-penalty rate becomes a parameter a regulator can set ex ante, and the sensor-fault rate at which the system may operate follows from it rather than from convenience.

7.3 The automation of administrative discretion

Sanitary inspection has never been mechanical enforcement: an officer may warn rather than fine, recognize a household in crisis, or distinguish a first lapse from a pattern. Lipsky (2010) showed that such discretion is not a defect in implementation but the place where policy is actually made. Bovens and Zouridis (2002) describe what happens when information systems absorb it: the street-level bureaucracy becomes a system-level bureaucracy, discretion migrates from the officer at the point of contact to the designer who wrote the threshold, and the constitutional controls attaching to official decisions do not migrate with it. Peeters and Widlak (2018) detail the consequences for citizens who cannot get an incorrect record corrected.

Our three-warning buffer is a deliberate, if crude, attempt to encode forbearance, but it does so uniformly, which is precisely what discretion is not. It cannot distinguish three lapses caused by indifference from three caused by hospitalization, and it is not obvious that it should try: a system that adjudicates hardship acquires a far larger surveillance footprint. The more defensible design reserves the automated tier for detection and evidence assembly and preserves a human waiver channel with recorded reasons, which is also what makes the resulting decisions reviewable.

7.4 Attribution, communal bins, and collective action

Household-level liability presupposes household-level attribution. In much of the target context, bins are communal, and a communal bin has the two properties that define a common-pool resource in Ostrom's sense (Ostrom, 1990): its capacity is subtractable, in that waste deposited by one household is capacity denied to the next, and exclusion is difficult, in that a bin on a public street cannot practically be restricted to registered users. Its observed state is therefore the joint product of many users' behavior, and no telemetry stream can decompose that state into individual contributions. The system can measure that a bin is overflowing; it cannot measure who overflowed it. Attribution therefore fails in one of two directions: either the breach is unattributable, and no enforcement follows, or it is attributed by proxy—nearest registered household, last recorded disposal—and some penalties are simply wrong, regardless of sensor accuracy.

This is a limit on instrument choice, not a gap to be engineered away. Where attribution fails, the appropriate instruments operate at the level at which the outcome is actually produced: ward-level service standards, collective incentives, and investment in provision, rather than individual fines. A deployment should therefore confine individual liability to bins with genuine single-user attribution and apply collective instruments elsewhere—a partition our current design does not make.

7.5 Distributive incidence and the informal recycling economy

A flat fine is regressive: the INR amounts in Equation 2 represent a materially different burden across income groups, and Ghimire et al. (2024) show that willingness to pay for unit-based waste tariffs in a comparable South Asian setting is both low and unevenly distributed. Eubanks (2018) provides the general pattern for automated administrative systems, which tend to concentrate their errors and their burdens on those least able to contest them.

There is a second, more specific distributive risk. A large share of the recycling actually performed in Indian cities is carried out by informal waste workers operating around and inside the municipal stream (Demaria and Schindler, 2016; Gidwani, 2015; Gutberlet, 2015; Doron and Jeffrey, 2018). A sensor-instrumented, penalty-bearing bin network can criminalize or displace that activity: by treating bin disturbance as tampering, by attributing bin-state anomalies to nearby households, or simply by formalizing a stream from which informal livelihoods are excluded. This is foreseeable and, in our view, the most serious social cost of the instrument, and it appears in no metric reported in Section 5. Instruments that integrate rather than displace informal workers—registration, cooperative contracting, and weight-based payment for delivered recyclate—exist in the literature (Gutberlet, 2015) and should be designed in from the start rather than retrofitted after displacement has occurred.

7.6 Procedural legitimacy and the limits of behavioral instruments

Deterrence is not the primary driver of compliance. Tyler (2006) shows that perceived procedural fairness predicts compliance more reliably than expected sanctions, and May (2004) distinguishes affirmative motivations, which erode when enforcement is experienced as arbitrary, from deterrence-based ones. The implication runs against the intuition that a technically more accurate enforcement system is necessarily a more effective one: a system that issues correct penalties through a process citizens experience as opaque and uncontestable can reduce compliance overall. Bardach and Kagan's account of regulatory unreasonableness, Bardach and Kagan (1982) describes the same dynamic, and the pyramid of Ayres and Braithwaite (1992) is a response to it.

The gamification layer carries a parallel risk. Yeung's “hypernudge,” Yeung (2017) describes a continuously updated, personalized behavioral score that shapes conduct without deliberation, which is a fair description of the Eco-Score. Vanolo (2014) argues that smart-city instruments of this kind shift responsibility for a structural service failure onto individual citizens, and Cardullo and Kitchin (2019) find that “smart citizen” participation is usually consumer-grade rather than political. A municipality that has not provided adequate collection capacity, and then scores households on their disposal behavior, is vulnerable to exactly this criticism. We take the implication to be that the incentive layer should be deployed only alongside a demonstrated improvement in service provision, and that its scoring rules should be public and contestable rather than tuned as an engagement mechanic.

7.7 Data protection, purpose limitation, and function creep

Linking per-bin telemetry to a household identifier to attribute penalties constitutes processing of personal data under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (Government of India, 2023): s. 2(t) defines personal data as any data about an identifiable individual, and the UID linkage is what makes the telemetry identifiable. Fill-level and weight series are moreover behaviorally revealing in ways a fill sensor's designers may not intend, communicating occupancy, absence, household size, and consumption patterns (Section 5.9). Edwards (2016) and Van Zoonen (2016) examine why smart-city telemetry resists conventional privacy governance: the data are collected for an uncontroversial operational purpose and acquire new purposes afterward.

That trajectory is visible in our own design. Telemetry justified by collection efficiency is reused for enforcement, which is a change of purpose, and the Act does not permit it to inherit the original basis. Section 4 prohibits processing except for a lawful purpose on a recognized ground, and s. 5 requires the notice accompanying consent to state the purpose for which the data will be processed, so enforcement must be specified as a purpose rather than arrive later. Section 8(7), which requires erasure once the specified purpose is no longer served, supplies a statutory basis for a retention limit rather than leaving it to good practice. The concrete requirements this implies—separating the identity store from the telemetry store, pseudonymous attribution resolvable only on appeal or audit, discarding sub-daily readings once the compliance window closes, and a published lawful basis naming enforcement—are stated in Section 5.9 and implemented in none of the prototypes.

7.8 Institutional capacity, fragmentation, and procurement

Even a lawful, fair, and privacy-respecting design fails if no organization can operate it. Kaza et al. (2018), and Guerrero et al. (2013) find institutional and financial arrangements, not technology, to be the binding constraint on waste outcomes in developing cities, and Meijer and Bolívar (2016) find that most smart-city initiatives change technology without changing governance arrangements. Three constraints are specific enough to state. First, responsibility is fragmented: sanitation departments, municipal IT functions, and contracted collection operators would each hold part of this pipeline, and the enforcement decision sits across the seam. Second, the five-year cost of ownership we report (Section 5.7) must survive annual municipal budget cycles and the incentive, familiar from the literature on digital-era governance Dunleavy et al. (2006), to procure a proprietary end-to-end platform whose data cannot be exported; an enforcement record that a citizen may need to contest should not be locked in a vendor's schema. Third, algorithmic accountability requires capacity that the deploying body may not have: Binns (2018), Veale and Brass (2019), and Janssen and Kuk (2016) all note that public bodies frequently cannot explain, audit, or contest the systems they operate. Publishing thresholds and fine schedules, maintaining an append-only decision log, and reporting wrongful-penalty and appeal-outcome statistics are the minimum, and all three are cheap to build if designed in and expensive to retrofit.

7.9 Implications for design: an evidentiary instrument first

Taken together, these constraints suggest a different deployment order from the one the architecture implies. The sensing, fog-tier alerting, and dynamic dispatch components address governance problems 1, 4, and 5 of Section 1.1 and raise comparatively modest regulatory difficulty: they improve service and generate the measurement-based performance standards and equity audits require. The compliance and gamification components address problems 2 and 3, but carry nearly all of the legal, procedural, and distributive risk analyzed above.

We therefore modify the claim the architecture makes. The defensible first deployment uses the compliance layer as an evidentiary and advisory instrument—building timestamped, contestable records that support human enforcement decisions and make service failures attributable—rather than as an autonomous penal one. Automated penalty execution should follow only once the statutory authority is explicit, an appeal mechanism with independent review is operating, attribution is restricted to genuinely single-user bins, income-sensitive calibration and informal-sector integration are in place, and a wrongful-penalty rate target has been set and is being measured against. This is a weaker claim than the original framing supported, and we take it to be the correct one.

8 Conclusion

This article proposes SWMS, a three-tier edge/fog/cloud architecture integrating multi-parameter bin sensing, fog-tier dynamic routing, and cloud-based compliance governance into one pipeline. The contribution is vertical integration rather than algorithmic novelty: no sensing, routing, or fog-placement technique here is new in isolation, but coupling all three with a graduated enforcement engine and a citizen gamification layer has not been demonstrated before.

Every quantitative result relies on a seeded, reproducible experiment. Fog-tier offloading cuts alert-to-actuation latency 7.5 × ; greedy+2-opt reaches a 5.1% gap to a proven optimum at sub-millisecond cost, matching the best tuned metaheuristic at three orders of magnitude less compute; telemetry-driven dispatch cuts daily distance 37.9% at matched overflow rates; scaling to 20,000 bins stays sub-quadratic; and fault injection quantifies the fog tier's ability to hold alert reliability under sensor degradation.

The system functions better as a policy instrument than as an optimizer. It targets five governance problems—service delivery decoupled from need with no accountability signal, a statutory segregation duty with no evidentiary base, ungraduated enforcement instruments, a hazard class the administrative cycle cannot serve, and the invisibility of the distributive burden (Section 1.1)—and its enforcement design implements the responsive-regulation pyramid rather than an ad hoc fine schedule. Reading it as an instrument also makes its constraints legible. Section 7 finds that statutory authority, technological due process, the automation of administrative discretion, attribution in communal bins, distributive incidence on informal waste workers, procedural legitimacy, data protection, and municipal capacity each bear on whether the compliance layer is lawful and administrable, and that a non-zero sensor error rate entails a non-zero wrongful-penalty rate that no filter removes. We therefore conclude that the compliance layer should first be deployed as an evidentiary and advisory instrument supporting human enforcement decisions, not as an autonomous penal one. This is a weaker claim than the architecture alone would support, and the one the analysis warrants.

That framing is intentional: a reproducible computational baseline with its gaps explicitly stated is more useful than claims that cannot be traced to executable experiments. The next steps are a hardware-in-the-loop deployment to validate the latency model against physical measurements, a structured household pilot—preferably under the regulatory-sandbox arrangement of Section 9.3—to replace simulated compliance figures with observed data, and integration of live traffic feeds. We release the experiment scripts and artifacts so future empirical studies can compare directly.

9 Limitations and future work

The conclusions of Section 8 rest on computational evidence and are bounded accordingly. We set out those bounds in three groups—the evidence base, the policy layer, and the regulatory analysis—and then describe the work that would remove them.

9.1 Current limitations

The first group concerns the evidence base. No physical prototype was built: the hardware parameters (Table 8) and cost figures (Section 5.7) rest on datasheets, retail pricing, and estimates, and the deviation we expect from sensor drift, load-cell vibration sensitivity, and long-term calibration drift has not been measured. The headline latency is analytical (Section 4.5); an executed iFogSim run and a queued SimPy model across all four load scenarios corroborate it to within ±25% (Section 5.2), but neither substitutes for instrumented hardware (Section 9.2). The distance saving holds on a real OpenStreetMap street network (Section 5.4), yet the objective remains shortest distance, not travel time under congestion: no live traffic feed reroutes a vehicle. Every study also assumes trusted sensors and links: telemetry spoofing and replay, sensor tampering, denial of service against a fog node, and record tampering are analyzed only qualitatively (Section 5.9), and no authentication, integrity, or intrusion-detection mechanism has been implemented or tested.

The second group concerns the policy layer. Its compliance and gamification mechanisms are simulated, not field-tested (Section 5.9); fine amounts were not checked against willingness-to-pay evidence for the target context [cf.Ghimire et al. (2024)], and their impact on low-income households was not assessed. Nor are the constraints identified in Section 7 implemented or modeled. Encryption-at-rest and anonymization for the household UID-to-telemetry linkage, appeal and human-review procedures, income-sensitive fine calibration and integration instruments for informal waste workers are all absent, and who would bear automated fines, given communal bins and income variation, is not simulated. Table 14 states what each would require, but stating a requirement is not the same as meeting it.

The third group concerns the regulatory analysis, which is conceptual rather than institutional. Section 7 draws on the literature alone: we have not obtained an administrative-law opinion on the delegation of penalty decisions, reviewed the bye-laws of any specific urban local body, or consulted municipal officials, sanitation workers, informal waste workers, or residents. The requirements in Table 14 are therefore analytically derived rather than validated, and each would need testing in a particular legal and institutional setting. The wrongful penalty estimate is likewise indicative. It maps overflow-alert false positives onto penalty events one-to-one, whereas the fine predicate spans four parameters and would filter further; it establishes that the rate is structurally non-zero and materially large but is not a calibrated forecast.

9.2 Hardware-in-the-Loop validation roadmap

Because the largest limitation is the absence of physical measurement, we regard a hardware-in-the-loop study as the single most important next step. Even a minimal study would answer questions no computational experiment can. It would measure behavior under the 5–30% packet loss realistic for urban NB-IoT and LoRa links, including whether threshold evaluation and route recomputation degrade gracefully, and when a fog gateway goes offline, including how edge bins buffer and resume telemetry. It would record real, non-stationary drift profiles for load cells and MQ-series gas sensors over weeks to months of field exposure, and battery state-of-charge across seasons and the maintenance-visit frequency the per-bin hardware requires (Section 5.7). It would also let the stack be hardened with encryption, authentication, and intrusion detection for a municipal deployment, while GPS-tracked vehicles would test whether simulated savings translate into real fuel and time savings under actual traffic.

9.3 Future directions

Several technical extensions follow from the results. The iFogSim run should be extended from the latency scenario to a full load sweep (balanced, stress, and energy) under a tuned tuple scheduler, and any divergence from the analytical model reconciled. The proven optimum of Section 5.3 quantifies the headroom a deep-reinforcement-learning routing policy could target—about 21 points over plain greedy and 5 over greedy+2-opt—although none was implemented here, and fog-tier routing should use live congestion data to optimize travel time rather than distance. Encryption-at-rest for the UID-to-telemetry linkage and an anonymization layer decoupling fine attribution from raw sensor history would meet the data-protection requirements of Section 7, and a permissioned blockchain could keep tamper-evident Eco-Score and fine records once the policy mechanism has field validation to record.

The policy layer, however, needs field evidence and institutional grounding more than further engineering. A structured household pilot modeled on Rosenlund et al. (2025) and Venturi et al. (2025) would replace the simulated Eco-Score and compliance figures with observed data, including fairness assessment across income groups and appeal-procedure design. Co-design with a single urban local body would test the requirements of Table 14 against its actual bye-laws, enforcement practice, and organizational capacity, ideally under a regulatory-sandbox arrangement in which the compliance layer runs in advisory mode and its proposed penalties are compared against the decisions human officers actually make; that comparison is the cheapest available test of whether the automated predicate tracks defensible enforcement. Finally, residents and, in particular, informal waste workers—whose livelihoods the instrument can displace (Section 7) and who are absent from every evaluation reported here—should shape its design before deployment rather than after.

Statements

Data availability statement

All results reported in this article are computational and reproducible from seeded scripts. The experiment code (experiments/, including latency_model.py, latency_des.py, routing_benchmark.py, routing_exact_and_tuning.py, routing_ real_roads.py, scalability_faults.py, sensor_calibration.py and fault_injection_calibrated.py), the iFogSim topology (SmartWasteManagementFog.java) and the JSON result artifacts on which every reported figure and table is based are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. Two third-party datasets are publicly available and were used unmodified: the UCI ‘Gas sensor array under dynamic gas mixtures' dataset (Fonollosa et al., 2015), used to calibrate the sensor error model, is available from the UCI Machine Learning Repository; the Chennai street network used in Section 5.4 is available from OpenStreetMap and was retrieved with OSMnx (Boeing, 2017). All bin-level telemetry used in this article is synthetic and generated by the seeded scripts listed above; no data from a physical deployment were collected.
